name: Acadesine

lead: Acadesine (AICAR) activates AMPK, a cellular energy sensor, and is promoted in fat-loss and performance circles as an exercise mimetic, with users hoping for greater fat burning and endurance without extra training.

Inside cells it is converted to an AMP-like molecule that activates AMPK, raising fat oxidation and glucose uptake in muscle in animal studies. A 2008 mouse study reported endurance gains. In humans it was tested for heart-surgery protection and some blood cancers, not fat loss, and the surgery trial stopped for futility.

paras: It is sold online as a research compound, and users add it alongside training and dieting in cutting phases. Reported routines are anecdotal, and no human body-composition protocol has been published.
It is not approved for body-composition use, and it has been on the WADA prohibited list since 2009. Human safety data for that use are lacking.

angle.text: Acadesine (AICAR) is promoted as an exercise mimetic: it activates AMPK, which raises fat oxidation in muscle in animal studies, and users hope for a leaner look without extra training. The idea comes from a 2008 mouse study.

lead: Acadesine, also called AICAR or AICA riboside, is a nucleoside that activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an enzyme that senses cellular energy status.[1][2] It was studied clinically for protecting the heart during surgery and in some blood cancers, and in 2008 a mouse study described it as an exercise mimetic, which led to interest from athletes and in online fat-loss and performance discussions.[3][2]
Human data for appearance or body-composition purposes are absent. The World Anti-Doping Agency has listed acadesine as a prohibited substance since 2009.[2]

paras: AICAR is taken up by cells and converted to a monophosphate that mimics AMP, activating AMPK.[1] In rat muscle, it increased AMPK activity, fatty acid oxidation and glucose uptake.[4] Activation of AMPK has also been reported to suppress muscle protein synthesis signaling via mTOR.[5]

Acadesine was first explored in the 1980s to preserve blood flow to the heart during surgery, and was developed by PeriCor Therapeutics and licensed to Schering-Plough in 2007. A phase III heart-surgery trial began enrolling in 2009 and was stopped in 2010 after an interim futility analysis.[2] In 2008 a Cell paper reported that AICAR improved endurance in sedentary mice, describing AMPK activators as exercise mimetics.[3]

Registered trials include a small 2002 trial of exercise-mediated glucose uptake in type 2 diabetes (n=40)[6] and a 1996 pilot study in two patients with Lesch-Nyhan disease.[7] Phase III testing in heart surgery was stopped for futility.[2] No studies of acadesine for fat loss or appearance in healthy people were found.

Acadesine is on the WADA prohibited list, and a 2009 BMJ report cited by Wikipedia said WADA found evidence of its use by cyclists.[2] It is sold online as a research chemical, and is described as an exercise mimetic in online fitness communities.
